body.statement: When \(S=\varnothing\), Branch-sCIDP and CIDP agree on the identification decision for \(P_{\mathbf M}(Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(X=x),C=c)\), and every successful Branch-sCIDP formula is equal pointwise on the represented observational-law domain to a CIDP identifying functional.
body.justification: The no-selection special case is the required regression against the settled conditional-PAG boundary.
body.gap: This is a sanity reduction rather than a novelty claim; it rules out a selected extension that changes the established no-selection answer.
body.consumer: PAGId retains its current CIDP behavior whenever no selection node is present.
body.proof_tex:
Assume \(S=\varnothing\).  The selection event is then the sure event, so Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}target\text{-}query}\) reduces to
\[
 \psi_{\mathbf M}(y;x,c)
 =P_{\mathbf M}(Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(X=x),C=c).
 \tag{1}
\]
In this specialization, \(\mathrm{lem{:}selected\text{-}rule\text{-}two}\) is the ordinary PAG Rule--2 equality because no selection coordinate occurs on either side.

Suppose first that CIDP succeeds.  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}cidp\text{-}no\text{-}selection\text{-}contract}\), it performs a finite sequence of legal Rule--2 moves of nonempty intersections with current buckets, reaches a role state \(\rho_\star=(\bar X_\star,\bar C_\star)\), and identifies the joint kernel
\[
 P_{\mathbf M}\!\left(
 Y,\bar C_\star\mid\operatorname{do}(\bar X_\star)
 \right).
 \tag{2}
\]
Every move in this sequence satisfies exactly the edge condition in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}reachable\text{-}role\text{-}graph}\).  Hence \(\rho_\star\in\Omega(\mathcal P;Y,X,C)\), and Branch-sCIDP visits it unless an earlier terminal call succeeds.  If sIDP returned \(\operatorname{Fail}\) at \(\rho_\star\), Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}sidp\text{-}completeness}\) would imply that the joint kernel (2) is not identified over the represented model class.  This contradicts the identification of (2) supplied by the CIDP contract.  Therefore sIDP succeeds at \(\rho_\star\), or Branch-sCIDP has already succeeded at an earlier visited state.  Thus CIDP success implies Branch-sCIDP success.

Conversely, suppose Branch-sCIDP succeeds.  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}branch\text{-}soundness}\) supplies an observed-law functional equal, throughout the represented positive discrete class, to the right-hand side of (1).  The conditional causal query is therefore identified.  Completeness in \(\mathrm{lem{:}cidp\text{-}no\text{-}selection\text{-}contract}\) rules out CIDP failure, so CIDP succeeds.  This proves agreement of the two identification decisions.

For the formula claim, let \(\Phi_{\mathrm B}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) denote any normalized functional returned by a successful Branch-sCIDP state, and let \(\Phi_{\mathrm C}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) denote the normalized joint functional returned by CIDP.  Branch soundness and the soundness clause of \(\mathrm{lem{:}cidp\text{-}no\text{-}selection\text{-}contract}\), respectively, imply that for every compatible positive discrete model \(\mathbf M\),
\[
 \Phi_{\mathrm B}(P_{\mathrm{obs},\mathbf M})
 =P_{\mathbf M}(Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(X=x),C=c)
 =\Phi_{\mathrm C}(P_{\mathrm{obs},\mathbf M}).
 \tag{3}
\]
Both normalizations are defined because the positive discrete model assumption makes their conditioning denominators positive; discrete marginalization, interpreted by countable additivity when a support is countably infinite, also covers the boundary cases \(C=\varnothing\) and an empty terminal conditioning role.  Equation (3) is precisely pointwise equality of the two functionals on the observational-law domain represented by \(\mathcal P\).  Hence every successful Branch-sCIDP formula is equal pointwise on that domain to a CIDP identifying functional.
